q: does the stop loss protect me overnight?
a: Partly. Swing positions keep a stop order at the broker overnight, but a stop can't sell in the middle of the night; it sells at the next open, wherever that is. Big overnight news, like an earnings report that moves a stock 10-20%, can gap right past it. That's why the swing desk doesn't buy within 3 trading days of an earnings report. At Alpaca, the overnight stop covers only whole shares, and the bot checks any fraction itself every 5 minutes. The day desk never holds overnight.

q: how far below the buy price are the stops?
a: Swing desk: a fixed 7% below what it paid, the stop it was tested with. Day desk: half the stock's usual daily range (its 14-day average true range), at least 1% and at most 5%; if the range is unknown, 2%. A wider stop buys a smaller position: no day trade loses more than 0.66% of the desk at its stop, and no position is bigger than 33% of the desk. Honest note: sizing stops to volatility is a common rule of thumb, not a tested edge.

q: what kind of orders does it send?
a: Normal buys and sells are limit orders set a hair through the price: 0.2% above the quote to buy, 0.2% below to sell. That way they fill fast but never at a crazy price. If a normal order isn't filled within 60 seconds, it's cancelled. Urgent exits, meaning a stop-loss, the day desk's end-of-day sell or an emergency stop, use market orders, because getting out comes first. Every position also gets a resting stop order at the broker.

q: why doesn't it just use market orders for everything?
a: Because a limit order caps the price. Kestrel's normal orders are limits 0.2% past the quote, so in the code's words they "fill fast, never at a crazy price". If one isn't filled in 60 seconds, the bot cancels it and then checks whether it filled at the last second. Market orders are kept for urgent exits only: a stop-loss, the day desk's end-of-day sell and the emergency stop. Those are left working until they fill, since getting out matters more than the exact price.

q: what if the internet cuts out right when it's placing an order?
a: The bot stops tracking an order only once the broker confirms it's finished (filled, cancelled, rejected or expired). If the broker can't confirm, it does nothing risky and checks again next cycle. Orders are written down the moment they're sent. At Alpaca and Webull they're written down with the bot's own tag before sending, so after a restart it can ask the broker whether it got that order. If an order went out but no order id came back, it tells you to check your account by hand.

q: could the bot accidentally sell the same shares twice?

q: what's a good faith violation?
a: It's a cash-account rule. You buy with money from a sale that hasn't settled yet, then sell that new stock before the money settles. Three in 12 months and Schwab restricts the account to settled cash for 90 days. Kestrel avoids it by only buying with settled money in a cash account, so every sale is safe. If a position was somehow bought with unsettled money (it shouldn't happen), it's held until that money settles. Only your typed emergency stop may sell it early, and that's counted.

q: when does money from a sale settle?
a: T+1: one business day after the trade. A business day here means the stock market is open and the banks are open. On Columbus Day and Veterans Day the market trades but the banks (the Federal Reserve) are closed, so nothing settles. When in doubt, Kestrel's settlement calendar says "not settled yet", because waiting a day costs nothing and a violation does.

Alpaca is treated as margin: every Alpaca account is a margin type, and Alpaca covers unsettled money itself, so there are no good faith violations there. You can set the account type in Setup → Settings. Kestrel never borrows either way.

q: what did the 16 year backtest actually show?
a: It tested methods from 2011 to 2026 with a $1,000 account, buying only, trading at the next day's open, with costs. Holding SPY made 14.0% a year (worst drop −33.7%). Holding QQQ made 18.9%, partly hindsight from tech's decade. Among funds, nothing simple beat holding SPY except QQQ. The SPY 200-day trend rule made 9.5% with a smaller worst drop (−21.7%): insurance, not profit. Momentum was the one stock method with real-world support, but realistically it's the market plus 1-2 points a year with bigger drops. The bot's old swing rules made only 0.7-1.6% a year.

q: so what were the backtest numbers for each method?
a: Per year, 2011-2026, $1,000 account: hold SPY 14.0% (worst drop −33.7%); hold QQQ 18.9% (−35.1%); sector rotation 12.0%; equal-weight S&P fund RSP 11.6%; SPY 200-day trend rule 9.5% (−21.7%); SPY 10-month rule 8.1%; dual momentum 6.2%; RSI-2 dip buying 2.9%. Stock picking, flattered by a survivors-only list: momentum top 10 40.5% (−44.2%), with a trend filter 29.9%. The bot's old rules: 1.6% and 0.7%. Fund results are trustworthy; the stock-picking ones are too high.

q: the backtest says momentum made 40% a year?? so that's what we'll get?
a: No. The 40.5% a year is flattered. The test's stock list only holds companies that survived and are popular today, and that hurts momentum most, since it buys stocks that went up, and in a survivors-only list those are the ones that kept going. q: why was momentum picked for stage 1?
a: Because it's the one stock-picking method with real-world support: a real momentum fund (MTUM), 30+ years of research, and the 16-year test. Most other ideas lagged holding SPY, including sector rotation, dual momentum, the monthly 10-month rule and RSI-2 dip buying, and the bot's old swing rules made about what Treasury bills paid. Momentum's real-world edge is modest, though: about the market plus a point or two, with bigger drops. Stage 1 checks it on paper before any real money.

q: what's the point of the 200-day average rule if it makes less money?
a: It's insurance. In the 16-year test, the SPY 200-day trend rule made 9.5% a year against 14.0% for just holding SPY, but its worst drop was −21.7% instead of −33.7%. It gave up 4-5 points a year to cut the worst fall. The research called that useful for sleeping at night and for protecting a small live account. That's why Stage 1's momentum only buys stocks above their 200-day average and makes no new buys while SPY is below its own.

q: what happened with the bot's original swing strategy?
a: It didn't work. On its watchlist of calm, cheap names, the old trend rule made 1.6% a year and the dip rule 0.7% over 2011-2026, about what short-term Treasuries paid (1.3%). In the 30-day windows test, the old trend rule made money and beat SPY only 8% of the time. The research concluded it must not be used as is, which is why Stage 1 switched to momentum.

q: does TJR's strategy actually work?
a: Not proven. On 16 years of daily stock charts, his long setups made +0.24R per trade, but random entries with the same stop and target made +0.18R, so the edge is small, and it shrank after 2018. Shorts lost (−0.24R). As an account it made 13.1% a year against 14.4% for SPY, and 9.0% against 14.4% in 2018-2026. His real method is intraday on futures, so this was only a rough check; the intraday test is still to do. Before Stage 2 paper trades it, a history test must pass: 30+ trades, profit factor 1.15+, making money, and beating random buys.

q: can 30 days of paper trading prove the strategy works?
a: No. The research checked every 30-trading-day window from 2011 to 2026. Even the best method (momentum top 10, in a flattered test) made money and beat SPY in only about 58% of them; momentum with the trend filter in about 49%; holding QQQ 47%. The bot's old trend rule managed 8%. So a 30-day stage can catch a broken method, but it can't prove a good one. Passing is evidence, not proof, which is why real money starts small.

q: if it passes paper trading does that mean it's a good strategy?
a: It means it cleared a bar, not that it's proven. In the 16-year research, even the best method failed a "make money and beat SPY over 30 trading days" test about 4 times in 10, so a good method can fail a stage and a lucky one can pass. What a stage reliably does is catch a broken method: the bot's old rules passed only 8% of the time. That's why passing leads to a small real-money test ($50), with more only if it makes money.

q: what's survivorship bias and why does it keep coming up?
a: The backtest's stock list only has companies that are still around and popular in 2026. Companies that didn't make it aren't in it, so any stock-picking rule looks better than it would have in real time. The yardstick: buying every stock on the list equally made 17.6% a year, while the real equal-weight S&P 500 fund (RSP) made 11.6%. That's about 6 points a year nobody could actually have had. Fund results like SPY and QQQ don't have this problem, so they're the trustworthy ones.

q: why does the swing desk hold 8 stocks instead of a few big ones?
a: In the bot's own 2011-2026 backtest, momentum with 8-10 holdings traded about 3 times as often as with 3, made about the same, and had a smaller worst drop (about −42% to −47%, against −57% with 3). So spreading out cost little and cut the worst fall. Each swing position is up to 12.5% of the desk's money, with a 7% stop-loss.

q: what's the stocks in play thing based on?
a: A 2024 paper by Zarattini, Barbon & Aziz (SSRN 4729284), on about 7,000 US stocks from 2016-2023. The 5-minute opening-range breakout made +3.2% a year on all stocks, but +41.6% a year on the top 20 by relative volume, meaning stocks trading far more than usual in their first minutes. Trades averaged −0.02R below 1x relative volume and +0.08R above it, and a 30-minute range did much worse than 5 minutes. So at 9:35am Kestrel adds the top 10 stocks at 1.0x or more to the day desk's list for that day.

q: 41.6% a year from the ORB paper sounds amazing, should we expect that?
a: No. The paper has big caveats: it was tested on the same data it was tuned on, it traded long and short, used 4x borrowed money, assumed no slippage, and used tight stops. Kestrel only buys and never borrows. So the bot tests the idea itself: orb_5min (the paper's rules, long only) is one of the day methods it compares in shadow trades, and the after-market report splits day trades into "in play" and "fixed list" so its own results show whether stocks in play actually help.

q: why does it skip buying stocks right before earnings? don't stocks usually go up around earnings?
a: You're right that on average they have: Frazzini & Lamont (2007) measured over 7% a year around earnings reports, though later work finds that premium has shrunk. Kestrel skips them anyway because a report can move a stock 10-20% overnight, past the 7% stop, and a stop can't sell overnight. So the swing desk doesn't buy within 3 trading days of a report. It's a safety choice, not a money-making one: it gives up some of that average for fewer big surprise losses. Setup → Settings turns it off.

q: does the earnings filter make kestrel more money?
a: Probably not, and it isn't meant to. Stocks have earned more around earnings reports on average (Frazzini & Lamont 2007 found over 7% a year, and later work finds it has shrunk), so skipping them gives a little of that up. What the filter buys is protection: a report can jump a stock 10-20% overnight, straight past a stop-loss. It's a safety choice that trades some average return for fewer big surprise losses.

q: will this make me rich?
a: Honestly, nobody can promise that, and Kestrel isn't built around getting rich. Its first job is to find out safely whether a strategy has an edge, and to say "don't trade" if it doesn't. The research's realistic expectation for its main method, momentum, is about the market plus 1-2 points a year, with bigger drops. Real money starts at $50 and grows only if it makes money. Most people who trade actively lose money. Past results don't guarantee future results, so only use money you can afford to lose.

q: can kestrel short stocks?
a: No. Kestrel only buys; it never sells short and never borrows. Your real-money plan couldn't short anyway: Alpaca only allows shorting with $2,000 or more of account equity, and only for easy-to-borrow stocks, while the plan is $50. q: would adding shorting make the ai better
a: Not proven, and the evidence leans against it right now. TJR's model tested on daily charts lost on its shorts (-0.24R per trade). The stocks-in-play breakout study traded both ways but never reported the short side on its own. For momentum, the short side is where 'momentum crashes' come from: beaten-down stocks rebound violently after a market drop (Daniel & Moskowitz, 2016). And a short's loss has no ceiling. The safe next step would be pretend-only short trades in the strategy comparison, which was proposed but isn't built yet.

q: why cant i short with my $50 alpaca account
a: Alpaca requires at least $2,000 of account equity to sell short (or to use margin at all), and even then only easy-to-borrow stocks can be shorted. A $50 account is far below that, so the broker itself won't allow it. Kestrel's other brokers, Schwab and Webull, are run as cash accounts, which can't short either. If shorting ever made sense, it would need $2,000 or more at a broker that allows it, plus evidence from pretend trades first.

q: whats a momentum crash
a: It's when a momentum strategy that owns the recent winners and is short the recent losers suddenly loses a lot. It usually happens right after a big market drop: the beaten-down losers rebound much harder than the winners, so the short side gets crushed exactly when the market recovers (Daniel & Moskowitz, Journal of Financial Economics, 2016). Kestrel's momentum method is long only, owning the strongest stocks, and buys nothing new while SPY is below its 200-day average, so it avoids the short side that causes those crashes.

q: isnt shorting how you make money when the market drops
a: It can be, but it carries risks Kestrel avoids. A short's loss has no ceiling because a stock can keep rising, and busy, fast-moving stocks can get squeezed. In Kestrel's own tests, TJR's shorts lost money. When the market is weak, Kestrel protects itself differently: the swing desk stops new buys while SPY is below its 200-day average, every position has a stop-loss, a desk down 3% in a day stops buying, and a desk down 15% from its best day sells everything.
